title: The god with the blue throat
hook: the ocean is churned, a poison rises, and Shiva drinks it; why Shivaratri is a night of pouring and keeping awake
carry: shiva drank the poison; we keep him company
tomorrow: The sign of the endless light

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi's goodbye: the clay given back to the water, and come early next year. Your line was visarjan: god stays when the clay goes.
screen: `GANESH CHATURTHI: VISARJAN: GOD STAYS WHEN THE CLAY GOES.`

segments.voice: The gods and the asuras, their old rivals, agree on one thing for once. Together they'll churn the ocean of milk and pull out amrita, the nectar that makes you immortal. A mountain for a churning stick. A giant serpent for a rope. But the first thing to rise out of the ocean isn't nectar. It's halahala, a poison so strong its fumes start to burn the worlds. Gods and asuras drop the rope and run. They run to Shiva. And Shiva, without a speech, cups the poison in his hand and drinks it.
screen: `THE OCEAN IS CHURNED.` → `A POISON RISES.` → `SHIVA DRINKS IT.`

segments.voice: In many tellings, Parvati, his wife, catches him by the throat so the poison can't go down, and there it stays, turning his throat blue. That's why Shiva is called Nilakantha, the blue-throated one, and why so many pictures show him with a blue neck. Hindus remember Shiva for it as the god who takes in what would destroy everyone else. Many families connect this story to Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva you met on day eighty-three. It's one of several reasons people give for the night. The day starts with a fast. At sunset the vigil begins, split into four watches called praharas, each about three hours, each with its own worship. All night comes abhisheka: water and milk, sometimes yogurt, ghee and honey, poured slowly over the Shiva lingam, with bilva leaves, three to a stem, laid on top. Many devotees say the cool pouring soothes the god who held fire in his throat. And there's jagarana, keeping awake. One telling says people stayed up that night singing to Shiva while he held the poison, and devotees still keep him company, chanting Om Namah Shivaya until dawn. So the vigil isn't just endurance. It's love for the one who swallowed the world's poison. And today: when someone you love is carrying something hard so the rest of you don't have to, Shivaratri's answer is simple. Don't leave them alone with it. Sit up with them.
screen: `NILAKANTHA: THE BLUE THROAT.` · `A FAST, THEN FOUR WATCHES.` · `ABHISHEKA: THE COOL POURING.` · `JAGARANA: KEEPING AWAKE.` · then, large: `DON'T LEAVE THEM ALONE WITH IT.`

segments.voice: Here's a Shivaratri practice you can do at home. Take a little water and pour it slowly, over a lingam if you have one, or into a bowl or onto a plant. If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya once with each pour. If you don't, just pour slowly and think of someone who's carrying something heavy right now. Breathe out as the water runs. Then sit for a minute and keep them company in your mind, the way a temple keeps Shiva company all night.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, kept awake with water and milk poured over the lingam, for the god with the blue throat.
Your line: shiva drank the poison; we keep him company. Nilakantha, the blue throat. Day one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a vigil through the four watches of the night, bathe the Shiva lingam with water, milk, yogurt, ghee or honey, offer bilva leaves, and chant Om Namah Shivaya until dawn; many remember Shiva as Nilakantha, who drank the poison from the churned ocean.
